bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Govt-payment cycle:** AMRUT funds not released (5-6 states) → UBR ballooned to 195d, WC to 166d; recurring (Jal Jeevan last yr, AMRUT this yr). Some releases now confirmed (Chhattisgarh; coming for Rajasthan/Haryana/MP).
- **Order finalization delays / re-bidding:** elongated bid evaluation; a Nov-Dec L1 project went to re-bid (timeline lost, neutral outcome).
- **Commodity / geopolitical crisis:** raw-material/lithium-ion cost spike → 1-2pp margin pressure.
- **Guidance credibility:** missed FY26 35% guidance; investor explicitly asked for realistic targets — FY27 deliberately conservative.
- **OCF post-tax negative** (-INR63 cr); concentration on central-govt-funded projects (de-risking via NTPC B2B + private wind).
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Candid on the miss — admitted revenue guidance not met, explained design-stage cost build-up, ECL/depreciation/IPP drags transparently. Conservative reframing of FY27 (42% conversion vs raw 75% growth). Took investor criticism on guidance realism gracefully. Confident but measured on renewables; disciplined leverage and capex discipline. Slightly defensive on "no margin compression" framing.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- The headline "+75% FY27 growth" is an artifact of a tiny FY26 base; mgmt insists on viewing it as ~42% OB conversion — the real number to track is conversion rate, not growth %.
- FY26 ~95% order-to-order conversion but revenue still missed — the bottleneck is design/approval-to-execution lag, not order wins.
- Renewables grew from ~INR12 cr (till Dec) to INR117 cr in Q4 alone — entire FY26 renewable revenue (INR129 cr) was back-ended and ~0-margin (IPP), structurally depressing Q4 optics.
- UBR at 195 days (not receivables — receivables actually improved to 53d) is the true working-capital story; it's GST-invoice timing tied to govt fund release, so a release wave could sharply unwind WC.
- Company is quietly building T&D/transmission pre-quals via BESS execution — optionality not yet priced.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Group snapshot states a debt-equity ratio of 0.34; the annual key-ratio chart shows debt to equity of 0.5 (FY23), 0.8 (FY24), 0.2 (FY25) and 0.3 (FY26), with debt of ₹645 / 2,336 / 2,341 / 4,223 Mn over the same years.
- Net worth has scaled sharply — ₹1,286 Mn (FY23), ₹2,922 Mn (FY24), ₹9,945 Mn (FY25, the IPO year) and ₹12,327 Mn (FY26) — while return ratios have compressed as the equity base grew: ROE 57.8% → 39.3% → 17.8% → 15.3% and ROCE 44.4% → 33.1% → 17.6% → 17.3%.
- Long-term borrowings rose to ₹2,473 Mn (Mar-26) from ₹983 Mn (Mar-25) and short-term borrowings to ₹1,750 Mn from ₹1,359 Mn, funding the PP&E and CWIP build; total assets grew to ₹20,422 Mn from ₹14,983 Mn.
- Credit ratings of CRISIL A/Stable (long term) and CRISIL A1 (short term); the wind segment is described as carrying near-zero debt with TD/TNW of 0.10.
- Working capital and liquidity as at Mar-26: trade receivables ₹1,653 Mn (down from ₹2,057 Mn), cash and cash equivalents ₹520 Mn (down from ₹1,624 Mn), bank balances ₹2,833 Mn (down from ₹3,928 Mn), other current financial assets ₹6,913 Mn (up from ₹3,792 Mn). The deck states no dividend or buyback policy.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- In-house design, engineering and process capability with specialised civil contractors only for site execution - stated to ensure quality control, reduce margin leakage and enable timely delivery
- Asset-light balance sheet discipline: debt-to-equity of 0.3x, kept well below 1.0x, with a selective HAM alongside EPC mix
- Track record moat: 57 projects and 958 MLD of cumulative treatment capacity since 2009, promoters with 53 years of cumulative experience and a 35+ year track record in water and wastewater management

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Total dependence on government funding cycles and policy priorities — The BRSR material-issues table states that all the projects executed by the Company are funded by Central or State Government schemes, so changes in policy or funding priorities may impact project flow; the MD&A threats section adds that unexpected delays in central fund disbursements or shifts in budget allocations - as witnessed historically in certain rural missions, and specifically cited as historical delays under the Jal Jeevan Mission - may temporarily impact working capital cycles. Mitigation claimed is diversification across states and funding mechanisms, and concentrating the order book on ring-fenced schemes such as AMRUT 2.0, Namami Gange and multilateral agency-funded projects.
- Working capital intensity of the EPC model — The business requires significant upfront investment in procurement, mobilisation, subcontracting and workforce deployment while collections are linked to milestone-based billing and certification. Delays in customer payments, release of retention money or extended approval cycles lengthen the cash cycle and raise funding requirements, and management notes that executing larger projects and expanding the business may raise working capital intensity further. The Company says it targets a 90-day working capital cycle and keeps debt-to-equity at 0.3x; the reported Debt Equity Ratio nevertheless moved from 0.24 to 0.34 (a 41.67% variance), attributed to better utilisation of borrowings.
- Cybersecurity, fraud and data integrity - a loss already crystallised in FY 2025-26 — This is not a hypothetical risk for EIEL: a cyber fraud incident occurred during the year, funds were traced and recovered through legal and banking channels, and the Company responded with a comprehensive overhaul of its IT security architecture, new SOPs, multi-tier authorisation protocols, multi-tiered digital firewalls, a review of financial approval workflows and mandatory continuous cybersecurity training. As operations digitise further, fraud attempts and data breaches remain a threat to financial and operational stability.
- Execution and operational complexity on increasingly large and technical projects — Executing complex ZLD systems and large-scale renewable EPC mandates carries risk of cost overruns, delays and third-party subcontractor failures. The stated mitigant is the fully in-house engineering, procurement and execution model that removes reliance on subcontractors - and management explicitly ties this to protecting its guided 22% to 24% EBITDA margins, so an execution slip transmits directly to the margin guidance. The BRSR material-issues table separately flags construction and execution risks covering project delays, cost escalation and supply chain disruption.
- Regulatory and environmental compliance under NGT and CPCB norms — The water and renewable sectors are highly regulated, with stringent discharge norms enforced by the National Green Tribunal and Central Pollution Control Board. The BRSR table notes non-compliance may lead to penalties, project delays or reputational impact, with negative financial implications from compliance costs and potential penalties. The Company relies on in-house design to build STPs and CETPs that exceed current standards, aiming to future-proof assets against evolving environmental law.
- Land acquisition, right-of-way and local clearance delays — Infrastructure projects inherently face delays in land acquisition, right-of-way approvals and local clearances - factors outside the Company's control that may extend execution timelines and, critically for an EPC recognising revenue on progress, delay revenue recognition.
- Grid non-availability, evacuation bottlenecks and technology obsolescence in the new renewable vertical — For the renewable ventures, delays in state-level grid infrastructure and transmission connectivity may affect timely commissioning and power evacuation for both IPP and EPC solar/wind assets. Separately, the rapid evolution of BESS and renewable hybrid technologies creates a technological obsolescence risk. Mitigation is a technology-agnostic approach with multiple leading global OEMs and rigorous pre-bid site assessments to confirm evacuation infrastructure before committing.
- Supply chain and raw material price volatility, plus interest rate exposure — As an infrastructure developer the Company is exposed to price movements in steel and cement and in specialised components such as RO membranes and BESS battery cells, mitigated through price escalation clauses in long-term contracts wherever feasible and strategic supplier tie-ups. Working capital borrowings are benchmarked to RBI-regulated reference rates such as REPO or Treasury Bills, so rate increases raise borrowing costs; interest rate scenarios are factored into project costing at the bidding stage.
- Credit concentration on public-sector receivables and intense competitive bidding — Credit risk arises mainly from receivables under EPC and O&M contracts executed for public sector clients - government bodies, urban development authorities and state-led infrastructure agencies - with contracts typically backed by budgetary allocations or multilateral funding. At the same time the attractiveness of the water utility and renewable sectors continues to draw domestic and international entrants, producing aggressive bidding environments that require strict margin discipline.

Wind EPC via **Suyog Urja Ltd** (acquired) — serves A-to-AAA-rated private clients. Solar assets + IPP. Reported as separate company; segmental revenues to be disclosed separately going forward.

business.body:
- Core business is described as designing, construction, operation and maintenance of Water and Wastewater Treatment Plants (WWTPs) and Water Supply Scheme Projects (WSSPs), delivered through three models — EPC, Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) and O&M.
- All projects are backed by Central and State Government bodies, with execution experience in World Bank-funded projects and participation in AMRUT, NMCG (National Mission for Clean Ganga) and SBM (Swachh Bharat Mission) schemes; the deck cites 'institution-backed projects with structured payment mechanisms ensuring revenue visibility'.
- Clientele listed as NMCG, Jal Nigam, industrial clients, municipalities and Public Work Dept.; marquee water counterparties include Maharashtra Urban Development Department, MIDC, UP Jal Nigam, Bihar Urban Infrastructure Development Corporation and Municipal Corporation Bhopal.
- Renewables arm is positioned across the value chain — 'Developer + EPC Contractor' for solar and BESS (IPP + EPC execution model) and 'End-to-End EPC contractor' for wind — with the NTPC relationship described as 'a landmark in grid-scale energy storage' and a strategic shift into thermal-linked BESS.

business.body:

- [Marquee renewable orders] 930 MWh BESS projects at 4 locations for NTPC (₹9,631 Mn), land/ROW/BOP including civil for CGE 30, an SPV of Continuum Green (₹2,075 Mn), 150 MWh BESS at Bihar for BSPGCL as BESS IPP (₹1,450 Mn), 29 MW (AC) Nagpur for MSEDCL (₹1,116 Mn) and 40 MW (AC) Odisha for SECI (₹645 Mn); wind ROW/civil work for ReNew, JSW Renew Energy (300 MW), Tata Power Renewable Energy, plus JSW 556 MW, ReNew 250 MW, Suzlon 50 MW and Vibrant Energy 25 MW projects.
- [Marquee water orders] STP & sewerage network Pune (₹4,976 Mn), 135 MLD STP Saharanpur for UP Jal Nigam (₹4,439 Mn), CETP Kolhapur upgradation with ZLD for MIDC (₹3,955 Mn), 20 MLD STP Bihar (₹3,483 Mn), STP & sewerage network Nashik (₹3,263 Mn), 60 MLD STP Bhopal (₹2,480 Mn), 60 MLD STP and sewerage scheme at Mathura (₹2,400 Mn) and 17+23 MLD STP Ramgarh, Jharkhand (₹2,054 Mn).
- [Government funding backdrop] Scheme outlay table (₹ Cr) shows JJM at 11,500 / 50,100 / 60,000 / 69,684 / 22,612 / 17,000 / 67,670, NMCG at 1,600 / 2,250 / 2,800 / 1,800 / 2,976 / 2,687 / 3,100 and AMRUT at 7,300 / 10,000 / 14,000 / 16,000 / 5,513 / 7,500 / 8,000 across FY20-21 actuals through FY26-27 budgeted; policy levers cited are AMRUT 2.0, Namami Gange, NRCP and NPCA. On the renewables side the deck cites India targets of 280 GW solar and 100 GW wind installed by 2030 with a 208 GWh BESS pipeline by 2030, installed solar of ~162 GW by June 2026 (26.3 GW added in H1 2026, +43% YoY), cumulative wind of 57.4 GW, a battery storage pipeline that has crossed 92 GWh backed by a ~₹5,400 crore VGF outlay (May 2026) for ~30 GWh of new capacity, and a non-fossil capacity share of 52% vs 30% in March 2015.
- [Revenue concentration] Q1FY27 state-wise sales mix is led by Maharashtra 29% (₹898 Mn), Madhya Pradesh 15% (₹646 Mn), Jharkhand 9% (₹338 Mn), Uttar Pradesh 9% (₹328 Mn), Chhattisgarh 8% (₹285 Mn) and Haryana 8% (₹275 Mn) — a marked shift from FY25 when Madhya Pradesh alone contributed ₹5,158 Mn.
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: EIEL designs, constructs, operates and maintains Water and Wastewater Treatment Plants (Sewage Treatment Plants, sewerage schemes and Common Effluent Treatment Plants) and Water Supply Scheme Projects (Water Treatment Plants with pumping stations and pipelines) for central, state and local government authorities, PSUs and urban local bodies, bidding on both EPC and Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) terms and retaining O&M contracts of 1 to 15 years after commissioning. Most of its STPs are Zero Liquid Discharge compliant and it is extending into tertiary treatment, water reuse and resource recovery such as Compressed Biogas from sludge. A second, independently managed vertical, housed in wholly owned subsidiary EIE Renewables Private Limited, covers solar EPC and IPP, utility-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems and, following the acquisition of Suyog Urja Limited, wind EPC.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Run two structurally separate growth engines - water and wastewater infrastructure on EBITDA-driven EPC and O&M economics, and renewable energy under wholly owned subsidiary EIE Renewables on EPC margins plus IRR-linked IPP returns - deliberately kept as independent operating and reporting units so different business models and risk profiles are not blurred.
- Move up the value chain by bidding for and executing larger, more technically complex projects with higher margin potential; execution capability has been expanded from 50 to 200 MLD for STPs and 20 to 50 MLD for CETPs.
- 'Value from Waste': convert tertiary-treated wastewater into a saleable resource for thermal power plants and process industries under NGT mandatory purchase obligations, rather than discharging it.
- Integrate Compressed Biogas plants within STP projects - purifying biogas from anaerobic sludge digestion for sale to oil marketing companies or on-site power - and classify/valorise sludge into Class A, B and C grades, turning a single-fee contract into a multi-revenue lifecycle platform.
- Grow the long-term O&M portfolio as an annuity layer that produces recurring revenue independent of new project awards and anchors client relationships over long cycles.
- Build a hybrid renewable platform spanning solar, BESS and wind - the last added post year-end through the Suyog Urja Limited acquisition - aimed at integrated, round-the-clock clean energy.
- Hold an early-mover position in BESS by clearing complex technical pre-qualifications for early utility-scale tenders, ahead of CEA-projected national storage requirements.
- Build a dedicated IPP asset portfolio (79 MW solar, 150 MWh BESS) evaluated on IRR, energy sales revenue and lease rental income rather than EBITDA, to add annuity-style cash flow beyond EPC cycles.
- Maintain asset-light financial prudence: selectively take HAM alongside EPC (targeting a 75:25 mix) while keeping debt-to-equity well below 1.0x.
- Embed instrumentation, automation and SCADA in build and operate phases - illustrated by sensor-driven, SCADA-managed Jal Jeevan Mission distribution infrastructure serving over 1,000 villages.
- Rebuild IT security architecture and SOPs after the FY 2025-26 cyber fraud, with multi-tier authorisation and continuous cybersecurity training across the organisation.
- Channel CSR through the Enviro Vatsalya Foundation for community health, poverty alleviation and employee volunteering, at a level the Company states goes well beyond the statutory minimum, plus welfare infrastructure for on-site labour.
- Diversify counterparty mix - Suyog Urja's clients are leading private sector energy developers and industrial groups, high-credit commercial counterparties that complement the Company's government-dominated water business.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: EIEL's expansion in FY 2025-26 was overwhelmingly platform- and acquisition-led rather than plant-capex-led, and the AR narrative describes it under 'Expansion Initiatives - Building New Platforms for Sustainable Growth'. In the core water business the Company continues to bid for and execute larger STP, CETP, sewerage and water-supply projects for government bodies, and is integrating Compressed Biogas (CBG) plants within STP projects to convert biogas from anaerobic sludge digestion for sale to oil marketing companies or on-site power generation, alongside advanced sludge treatment that classifies bio-solids into Class A/B/C resources for fertiliser or energy use. It is also building the commercial framework to resell tertiary-treated wastewater to thermal power plants and process industries under NGT-mandated purchase obligations, and is targeting ZLD mandates enabling industrial clusters to reuse more than 90% of treated wastewater. The second leg is the renewable platform under wholly owned subsidiary EIE Renewables: a solar portfolio scaled to 91 MW comprising 79 MW of IPP solar and 12 MW of EPC solar, which includes a recently acquired 40 MW IPP solar asset in Bolangir, Odisha and a 29 MW project under execution for MSEDCL in Maharashtra that carries state financial assistance of INR 32 million per MW and a 25-year PPA. In storage, EIEL secured four NTPC EPC orders aggregating 930 MWh and has commissioned a 150 MWh BESS IPP asset, for a combined 1,080 MWh portfolio. Wind was added post year-end through EIE Renewables' acquisition of Suyog Urja Limited for INR 3,110 million - described as asset-light and zero-debt - bringing 1,200 MW of completed wind execution experience, an active pipeline of 1,702 MW and an order book of approximately INR 7,770 million. The corporate structure was expanded accordingly during and after the year: EIE Renewables Private Limited (7 May 2025), Sunaxis Renewables Private Limited (6 June 2025), Soltrix Energy Solution Private Limited (25 June 2025, holding a 29 MW AC solar project), Vento Power Infra Private Limited (20 August 2025), and post year-end PRA Bihar Bess Private Limited (21 April 2026) and Suyog Urja Limited (28 April 2026). The recurring O&M portfolio stands at INR 9,506 million on contracts of up to 15 years post-commissioning. No rupee capex quantum is stated anywhere in this bundle: the capital-commitments named disclosure carries only its label line with no figure.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- A substantial portion of the order book was in design, engineering and early mobilisation during FY 2025-26 - stages that are capital and management-intensive but contribute minimally to revenue recognition; as construction advances through FY 2026-27, revenue recognition is expected to mirror the scale of the underlying order book.
- EBITDA margin of 24.2% is described as consistent with the Company's stated guidance for the water and wastewater segment.
- Structural water demand: the Indian wastewater treatment market is supported by an estimated immediate bid pipeline exceeding INR 26,000 crore under AMRUT 2.0 alone, and the sector is described as structurally positioned for sustained double-digit growth.
- The future landscape is expected to be dominated by Hybrid Annuity Models and 'One City, One Operator' frameworks, enabling long-term operational efficiency and stable annuity yields for EPC players.
- NGT enforcement of stringent ZLD guidelines and mandated purchase of treated sewage water by thermal power plants is expected to raise industrial demand for complex tertiary treatment and desalination equipment.
- Centrally funded missions - AMRUT 2.0 (INR 2.77 lakh crore outlay, mandating cities meet at least 20% of water demand and 40% of industrial water demand from reuse), Namami Gange Phase-II (INR 22,500 crore through 2026, HAM and 15-year O&M), and SBM-U 2.0 (INR 1.41 lakh crore, FSSM in Tier 2/3 cities) - provide long-term visibility and execution scale.
- Sector shift from disposal to recycling, reuse and resource recovery: sludge classification and valorisation, resale of tertiary-treated water, and on-site biogas/rooftop solar energy integration to offset aeration and pumping energy costs.
- Renewables: India targets 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030; the CEA projects a requirement of nearly 42 GW (208 GWh) of BESS capacity by FY 2029-30, and Viability Gap Funding supports early BESS project viability.
- The renewable sector is moving beyond standalone solar parks towards hybridisation and storage; developers able to integrate wind, solar and BESS gain a competitive advantage through 24/7 supply and reduced grid imbalance.
- Wind: India's cumulative installed wind capacity crossed 56 GW by end FY 2025-26 with a record 6.05 GW added, against a government target of 100 GW by 2030, with the pipeline increasingly shaped by Wind-Solar Hybrid tenders.
- Threats management flags as affecting the outlook: land acquisition, right-of-way and clearance delays extending execution timelines; grid non-availability and evacuation bottlenecks delaying renewable commissioning; dependency on government funding cycles affecting working capital; and intense competition producing aggressive bidding that requires strict margin discipline.
- Consolidated order book of INR 68,136 million entering FY 2026-27, up 242% year-on-year, driven by key water EPC wins and the addition of the Suyog Urja order book.
- The year opened with an order book of approximately INR 11,855 million, most of which was still progressing through design, engineering and early mobilisation.
- O&M portfolio at INR 9,506 million, covering long-term contracts that generate recurring, annuity-based revenue independent of new project awards.
- Major FY 2025-26 order wins: INR 3,955 million ZLD CETP for MIDC in Maharashtra, INR 3,484 million STP project from Bihar Urban Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd., and INR 2,480 million urban sewerage project from Municipal Corporation Bhopal.
- Renewable orders: four NTPC BESS EPC contracts aggregating 930 MWh across Uttar Pradesh, Assam, Karnataka and Telangana, plus a 150 MWh BESS IPP asset (1,080 MWh combined).
- Suyog Urja brings an order book of approximately INR 7,770 million and an active wind execution pipeline of 1,702 MW.
- Management states the healthy order pipeline and disciplined execution provide strong forward visibility, with existing order inflows supporting medium-term growth expectations under conservative conversion assumptions.

deepdive.thesis: Pure-play water/wastewater EPC missed FY26 revenue guidance (35%→7.5% growth) on slow order finalization + projects stuck in design stage, but pivots hard into renewables (BESS/wind/solar, now ~35-40% of order book) with all-time-high INR6,814 cr total order book giving ~24-month visibility — execution conversion (not order book) is the swing factor, and a global commodity crisis trims FY27 margin guidance.

risks.note: The BRSR material-issues table states that all the projects executed by the Company are funded by Central or State Government schemes, so changes in policy or funding priorities may impact project flow; the MD&A threats section adds that unexpected delays in central fund disbursements or shifts in budget allocations - as witnessed historically in certain rural missions, and specifically cited as historical delays under the Jal Jeevan Mission - may temporarily impact working capital cycles. Mitigation claimed is diversification across states and funding mechanisms, and concentrating the order book on ring-fenced schemes such as AMRUT 2.0, Namami Gange and multilateral agency-funded projects.
risks.risk: Total dependence on government funding cycles and policy priorities

risks.note: The business requires significant upfront investment in procurement, mobilisation, subcontracting and workforce deployment while collections are linked to milestone-based billing and certification. Delays in customer payments, release of retention money or extended approval cycles lengthen the cash cycle and raise funding requirements, and management notes that executing larger projects and expanding the business may raise working capital intensity further. The Company says it targets a 90-day working capital cycle and keeps debt-to-equity at 0.3x; the reported Debt Equity Ratio nevertheless moved from 0.24 to 0.34 (a 41.67% variance), attributed to better utilisation of borrowings.
risks.risk: Working capital intensity of the EPC model

risks.note: This is not a hypothetical risk for EIEL: a cyber fraud incident occurred during the year, funds were traced and recovered through legal and banking channels, and the Company responded with a comprehensive overhaul of its IT security architecture, new SOPs, multi-tier authorisation protocols, multi-tiered digital firewalls, a review of financial approval workflows and mandatory continuous cybersecurity training. As operations digitise further, fraud attempts and data breaches remain a threat to financial and operational stability.
risks.risk: Cybersecurity, fraud and data integrity - a loss already crystallised in FY 2025-26

risks.note: Executing complex ZLD systems and large-scale renewable EPC mandates carries risk of cost overruns, delays and third-party subcontractor failures. The stated mitigant is the fully in-house engineering, procurement and execution model that removes reliance on subcontractors - and management explicitly ties this to protecting its guided 22% to 24% EBITDA margins, so an execution slip transmits directly to the margin guidance. The BRSR material-issues table separately flags construction and execution risks covering project delays, cost escalation and supply chain disruption.
risks.risk: Execution and operational complexity on increasingly large and technical projects

risks.note: The water and renewable sectors are highly regulated, with stringent discharge norms enforced by the National Green Tribunal and Central Pollution Control Board. The BRSR table notes non-compliance may lead to penalties, project delays or reputational impact, with negative financial implications from compliance costs and potential penalties. The Company relies on in-house design to build STPs and CETPs that exceed current standards, aiming to future-proof assets against evolving environmental law.
risks.risk: Regulatory and environmental compliance under NGT and CPCB norms

risks.note: Infrastructure projects inherently face delays in land acquisition, right-of-way approvals and local clearances - factors outside the Company's control that may extend execution timelines and, critically for an EPC recognising revenue on progress, delay revenue recognition.
risks.risk: Land acquisition, right-of-way and local clearance delays

risks.note: For the renewable ventures, delays in state-level grid infrastructure and transmission connectivity may affect timely commissioning and power evacuation for both IPP and EPC solar/wind assets. Separately, the rapid evolution of BESS and renewable hybrid technologies creates a technological obsolescence risk. Mitigation is a technology-agnostic approach with multiple leading global OEMs and rigorous pre-bid site assessments to confirm evacuation infrastructure before committing.
risks.risk: Grid non-availability, evacuation bottlenecks and technology obsolescence in the new renewable vertical

risks.note: As an infrastructure developer the Company is exposed to price movements in steel and cement and in specialised components such as RO membranes and BESS battery cells, mitigated through price escalation clauses in long-term contracts wherever feasible and strategic supplier tie-ups. Working capital borrowings are benchmarked to RBI-regulated reference rates such as REPO or Treasury Bills, so rate increases raise borrowing costs; interest rate scenarios are factored into project costing at the bidding stage.
risks.risk: Supply chain and raw material price volatility, plus interest rate exposure
